subject.title: After Reverdy
subject.author: Ron Padgett
subject.text:
I would never have wanted to see your sad face again
Your cheeks and your windy hair
I went all across the country
Under this humid woodpecker
Day and night
Under the sun and the rain

Now we are face to face again
What does one say to my face

Once I rested up against a tree
So long
I got stuck to it
That kind of love is terrible

title: Forty-Two Years Between a Joke and a Translation
standfirst: In April 1964, twenty-one-year-old Ron Padgett published something called Some Bombs (Mistranslations) (after Reverdy). Five years later he opened his first book with a six-line poem carrying the same borrowed name. The real translation took until 2007.

sections.heading: Not the First Time He Put Reverdy's Name on Something
sections.body: The six lines above are not the first time Ron Padgett put Pierre Reverdy's name on a poem of his own. Five years earlier, in April 1964, the twenty-one-year-old Padgett published something called *Some Bombs (Mistranslations) (after Reverdy)* across four pages of the eighth issue of [C: A Journal of Poetry](https://www.granarybooks.com/pages/books/3201/ted-berrigan-ed/c-a-journal-of-poetry-vol-1-no-8-april-1964), the mimeographed magazine Ted Berrigan ran out of a cheap New York apartment. When Padgett gathered his first full collection, *[Great Balls of Fire](https://www.abebooks.com/9780918273802/Great-Balls-Fire-Padgett-Ron-0918273803/plp)*, in 1969, both poems made the cut. The magazine piece went in under a shorter title, its subtitle — the word *mistranslations* — quietly dropped. This one went first: not buried mid-book, but the poem the whole collection opens on.

sections.heading: A Discovery Story That Doesn't Quite Line Up
sections.body:
Padgett's own account of meeting Reverdy tells a cleaner story. In the [postface](https://nonsite.org/article/hearing-the-tone-of-the-self-toward-an-alternative-ethics-of-translation-2) to *Prose Poems*, his 2007 translation of Reverdy's first book, he places the real beginning in 1965, on a Fulbright year in Paris, where he read *Poèmes en prose* and, in his own words, loved its "austerity, its spookiness, and what I imagined to be its cubism." He decided on the spot to translate the book, drafted it while still in France, and then — his account says — worked at it on and off for the next twenty-five years.

That story has a problem: it starts a full year after Padgett had already put Reverdy's name on a poem in print. Either the postface simplifies a longer, messier acquaintance — Reverdy had already been translated into English by Kenneth Rexroth and others through the 1950s, so an American student could easily have met him first in someone else's English before meeting him in his own French — or the two "afters" describe two different kinds of contact: a game played with a poet's reputation in 1964, a real reading of his actual sentences a year later. Nothing Padgett has published settles which.

sections.heading: From the Bateau-Lavoir to a Wall Near a Monastery
sections.body:
The poet on the other end of both titles had already lived several careers by the time Padgett found him. [Pierre Reverdy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Reverdy) arrived in Paris from Narbonne in 1910 and fell in with the painters at the Bateau-Lavoir in Montmartre years before the movements that grew out of that building had settled on their names. In 1917 he founded and edited *Nord-Sud*, a small magazine that ran for sixteen issues and gave Cubism, and the poetry written alongside it, a shared page for the first time. André Breton later called him the greatest poet of the age.

From 1921 to 1926 Reverdy was also the lover of Coco Chanel, already one of the most famous women in France; the romance cooled but the friendship did not, and in 1960, sensing he was close to death, he wrote her a poem naming a love that had lasted forty years. In between, in 1926, he converted to Catholicism, burned a quantity of his own manuscripts, and moved with his wife, Henriette, into a house against the wall of the Benedictine abbey at Solesmes, where he lived a near-monastic life for the next three decades.

sections.heading: A Woodpecker That May Once Have Been a Peak
sections.body:
Whatever "After Reverdy" is exactly — translation, imitation, dare — it borrows more than a name. It carries no punctuation at all, not even a closing full stop, which lets its three unevenly sized stanzas (six lines, then two, then four) run together as one held breath rather than a set of finished sentences. Its phrasing keeps a slightly foreign cadence: "your cheeks and your windy hair" reads like English still carrying the shape of a French sentence behind it, wind-blown hair translated a beat too literally into hair that belongs to the wind.

The strangest image in it, "under this humid woodpecker," is also the hardest to place on its own terms — nobody actually stands under a woodpecker for weather. In French, *pic* means both woodpecker and mountain peak; a humid *pic* makes ordinary sense as a wet peak looming over a landscape, exactly the kind of plain, concrete image Reverdy built whole poems from, and almost none as a bird. Whether that is what happened here is impossible to prove without knowing which Reverdy lines, if any, these six stanzas are answering — Padgett has never said, in anything that has surfaced in print. But a poem that once wore the word *mistranslation* in its title is at least an invitation to read the wrong word as the point rather than the mistake.

sections.heading: Forty-Two Years to Decide on a Comma
sections.body:
The actual translation Padgett had promised himself in 1965 took most of a working life to finish. *Prose Poems*, his rendering of Reverdy's *Poèmes en prose*, was not published until 2007 — Black Square Editions and The Brooklyn Rail brought it out forty-two years after that Fulbright year, after a burst of revision in the early 1990s, a few magazine excerpts, and long stretches when the manuscript simply sat untouched. Even that late, Padgett kept adjusting the smallest things. His [postface](https://nonsite.org/article/hearing-the-tone-of-the-self-toward-an-alternative-ethics-of-translation-2) notes that Reverdy's French punctuation, carried straight across into English, read as "quirky in English" rather than the plain style Reverdy actually worked in, since, in Padgett's own summary, "Reverdy was a modernist, but he was not one for giving effects." Semicolons became commas. A comma splice that would be a mistake in careful English was left standing, because it sounded like someone talking rather than someone punctuating.

None of that scruple is anywhere in the six lines above. The poem that carried Reverdy's name into Padgett's first book was written by someone still young enough to treat translation as raw material for a poem of his own, not a debt owed back exactly.

sections.heading: Born on the Day Reverdy Would Die
sections.body:
One coincidence neither man arranged: Padgett was born on the 17th of June, 1942. Reverdy died on the 17th of June, 1960 — eighteen years later, the same calendar date. It proves nothing, but it makes "after Reverdy" sound, for one line of a birth certificate, almost literal.

By 1960 Reverdy had spent thirty-four years behind the abbey wall he chose in 1926, tied to a devotion he never fully renounced even when it plainly cost him — his own late poem to Chanel names a love he had carried for forty years and still could not walk away from. Padgett's six lines close on an image that now reads like an unintended description of both men's attachments: someone who rests against a tree "so long" that he "got stuck to it," followed by the flattest judgment in the whole poem — that kind of love is terrible. Reverdy earned that line on the evidence of his own life, about God and about Chanel both. Forty-two years and one very small comma later, it is hard not to read it as Padgett's too.
